claims.text: The starting material is an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy.
The alloy can be produced from hydride/elemental powder blends by vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h.
Hydride/elemental powder processing inherently introduces approximately 0.5 wt.% or less oxygen into the alloy.
Tailoring hydride precursor selection and processing atmosphere can control the alloy oxygen content at approximately 1.0 wt.%.
High-temperature compression testing in approximately the 750–1100 °C range is applicable to this alloy.
Oxidation behavior can be evaluated at approximately 1000 °C under flowing air.
Dual-beam irradiation conditions are relevant for evaluating this alloy's irradiation stability.
At approximately 1.0 wt.% oxygen, oxygen atoms will be distributed interstitially within a single-phase beta-BCC matrix.
Interstitial oxygen impedes dislocation motion and thereby provides solid-solution strengthening.
Controlling oxygen near 1.0 wt.% prevents excessive stabilization of secondary phases such as alpha-HCP.
Excessive secondary-phase formation could compromise thermal or irradiation stability.
When combined with a silicide coating, the oxygen-modified microstructure supports self-healing oxidation behavior.
An alloy containing approximately 1.0 wt.% oxygen will have significantly higher yield strength than a lower-oxygen control.
An alloy containing approximately 1.0 wt.% oxygen will have significantly higher hardness than a lower-oxygen control.
The approximately 1.0 wt.% oxygen alloy will retain oxidation resistance comparable to that of the lower-oxygen baseline.
The approximately 1.0 wt.% oxygen alloy will retain irradiation stability comparable to that of the lower-oxygen baseline.
Oxygen contents above approximately 1.0 wt.% may cause undesirable alpha-HCP or other secondary phases.
Secondary phases formed above the proposed oxygen limit may degrade mechanical and thermal properties.
